9 Some other observations

The darkest hexagons appear mostly around groups of eldercare centres. The far western and eastern edges remain lighter across all three maps.
KD2SFCA produces sharper local changes because a facility stops contributing once it falls outside the five-kilometre catchment.
One Central Region hexagon has a much larger SAM value than the rest. It stretches the vertical scale and makes the other regional boxes look flatter.
Each map uses its own quantile breaks. The shades show relative ranking within a map, so the same blue does not represent the same accessibility value across methods.

title: Conflict across Myanmar’s townships
text:
127 townships recorded increases

Kawkareik, Kyaukpyu and Nawnghkio had the largest rises. Kyaukpyu added 207 events, while its neighbours averaged 53 fewer and Rakhine’s total fell by 734.

Over the full study period, Maungdaw ranked 17th by incidents but third by reported deaths: 599 events and 1,583 deaths. Kale had the highest reported death toll, at 1,877.

Reported deaths include civilians and combatants. Zero can mean that fatality information was unavailable. Full fatality comparison

title: Conflict across Myanmar’s townships
section: Maungdaw ranks higher for reported deaths
text:
Maungdaw ranks higher for reported deaths

Maungdaw ranks 17th by incidents but third by reported deaths, with 599 events and 1,583 deaths. Kale has the highest reported death toll, at 1,877. Counting incidents alone would give Maungdaw much less attention.

Reported deaths include civilians and combatants. ACLED also records zero when fatality information is unavailable.

title: Conflict across Myanmar’s townships
text:
New hotspots around Kawkareik

The number of hotspots fell from 27 to 18. Yet five of the seven appearing only in 2025 border Kawkareik. Nearby Hlaingbwe rose from one to 41 events and still qualifies after adjustment for multiple tests. The increase extends across neighbouring townships.

Both maps use January to September and the same neighbours. They compare hotspot labels, without directly testing whether the change between years is significant.

title: Conflict across Myanmar’s townships
text:
Conflict and continuing needs
After the February 2021 coup, fighting spread into central Myanmar alongside the long-running conflicts in border states. By September 2025, close to 3.6 million people were displaced. Restrictions on movement and aid access disrupted daily life. OCHA, September 2025
The report follows 53,805 recorded events across 330 townships over 57 months, from January 2021 to September 2025. It asks:

Where did conflict cluster, and how did those concentrations change?
Which forms of violence increased, especially those targeting civilians?
Where did civilian targeting keep recurring?

Township maps locate clusters and outliers. Monthly hotspot histories follow changes in both total events and civilian targeting, with checks for different neighbours, comparison periods and related months.

Includes battles, explosions/remote violence and violence against civilians. Data: ACLED Myanmar, supplied through eLearn; MIMU v9.4. Conflict background.

title: Conflict across Myanmar’s townships
section: The monthly total peaked in late 2023
text:
The monthly total peaked in late 2023

The monthly total peaked at 1,465 events in November 2023, shortly after Operation 1027 began.
January to September 2025 recorded 8,728 events, compared with 9,961 in the same months of 2024: a 12.4% decline. The township comparisons show how unevenly that decline was shared.

title: Conflict across Myanmar’s townships
section: Most hotspots are in central Myanmar
text:
Most hotspots are in central Myanmar




Gi* identifies neighbourhoods with unusually high or low counts: 38 hotspots and 53 coldspots. Sagaing, Mandalay and Magway contain 31 of the hotspots.
Local Moran’s I compares each township with its neighbours. It finds 38 high-count clusters, 52 low-count clusters and four low-count outliers beside higher-count neighbours.
The civilian map has 37 hotspots, including 34 from the overall map. Hakha, Tonzang and Nawnghkio appear only in the civilian map.

Neighbours share an edge or corner; permutation p < 0.05. Adjustment for multiple tests reduces overall hotspots to 19. Six-nearest neighbours retains 87.2% of labels among the 327 townships with Queen neighbours; precise locations retain 91.7%. Tonzang has two civilian-targeting events, so its label mainly reflects neighbours.

title: Conflict across Myanmar’s townships
text:
How hotspot patterns changed




EHSA follows neighbourhood concentrations through time:

26 oscillating hotspots; 21 had cold months only in early 2021.
Eight sporadic hotspots: hot on and off, ended hot, and never cold.

The mapped 23 hotspots and 42 coldspots also pass the trend test. With the original reference, the stricter checks retain rising trends in Kawkareik and Nawnghkio.
Monywa missed the September 2025 threshold, ending with “No pattern detected” after many hot months.

Accounting for related months reduces significant trends from 218 to 148; 126 survive multiple-test adjustment. Comparing against the same two months retains 85.9% of EHSA classes. Reference check

text:
Air/drone events and abductions increased
The four largest changes in civilian-targeting events, January to September:

Civilian targeting fell only 2%, from 2,911 to 2,854 events. Air/drone events rose from 580 to 875, and abductions from 386 to 736. Declines in shelling and other categories offset these increases.
Kyaukpyu had the largest civilian-targeting air/drone increase, from 6 to 40. In 26 townships, including Myaing and Pakokku, civilian targeting rose while total events fell.

Both years cover the same nine months. Counts describe recorded events; one event can involve several strikes or people abducted. All recorded actors are included.

title: Conflict across Myanmar’s townships
section: Stricter checks narrow the hotspot list
text:
Stricter checks narrow the hotspot list

Allowing for chance findings across many tests reduces the overall hotspot count from 38 to 19.
Using the six nearest townships as neighbours keeps 87.2% of classifications unchanged among townships with shared-boundary neighbours.
Accounting for similarities between nearby months reduces significant trends from 218 to 148. 126 remain after also allowing for the number of tests.
Kawkareik and Nawnghkio still show rising concentrations after these checks.

Reporting coverage, approximate locations and township size affect the counts. The maps show recorded conflict; assessing current safety also needs local information.

title: Take-home Exercise 2
text:
2 Background to the conflict

2.1 The coup and the groups involved
Myanmar entered 2021 with a long history of armed conflict. Ethnic armed organisations had fought the military over autonomy and political power, particularly in border regions. These conflicts continued alongside the new resistance that emerged after the military seized power on 1 February 2021. Brenner and Han, 2022; ACLED
Protests against the coup met violent repression. Some protesters sought military training from established armed groups, while communities formed local defence forces. Fighting spread into central areas that had previously experienced relative peace.







Group
Who they are




Myanmar military
The armed forces that seized power in 2021 and fought resistance groups across the country.


Ethnic armed organisations
Established armed groups seeking greater control over their regions and a say in national politics. The Arakan Army in Rakhine is one example.


People’s Defence Forces
Resistance groups formed after the coup. Some trained and fought alongside ethnic armed organisations.



Cooperation varied from place to place. Groups opposing military rule could still disagree over territory, resources and who should govern. This helps explain why the conflict involved different combinations of armed groups across regions. ACLED’s account of resistance groups


2.2 Changes in the fighting
Fighting spread to new areas, and the weapons and tactics also changed. Three developments help explain the period covered by the maps:




Period
Development




October 2023
The Brotherhood Alliance, a coalition of three ethnic armed organisations, launched Operation 1027 in northern Shan. Attacks extended across several townships, including Lashio and Nawnghkio. ACLED


2024
The military increasingly used airstrikes against civilians. In February, it began enforcing a law requiring compulsory military service, and abductions for forced recruitment increased. Other armed groups also carried out forced recruitment. ACLED


By May 2025
Both military and resistance forces used drones. The military expanded its drone operations alongside aircraft and helicopters, including in fighting around Nawnghkio and Kawkareik. ACLED’s July 2025 report



These developments give a reason to look beyond the total number of events. Fewer battles can occur alongside more air attacks or abductions. The later comparisons follow each recorded form of violence separately.


2.3 Civilian life during the conflict
For civilians, control over an area could be confusing and changeable. In parts of Rakhine, people dealt with both the military administration and the Arakan Army. One authority might provide justice while another funded schools and healthcare. Interviews conducted in 2023, published in 2025, describe how money, personal connections and ethnic identity affected people’s ability to negotiate demands or avoid contact. Weigand and colleagues, 2025
By late 2024, families across Myanmar faced food shortages, lost livelihoods and severely disrupted public services. In September 2025, checkpoint delays and transport blockades still restricted access to assistance, while funding gaps left many people without sustained support. OCHA, December 2024; OCHA, September 2025
A lower event count therefore leaves questions about people’s daily circumstances. Alongside the hotspot maps, this report follows how often civilian targeting was recorded in each township, including places where recent totals fell.

title: Take-home Exercise 2
text:
8 Reading the findings together
The three study questions lead to the following findings:







Study question
Main finding




Where did conflict cluster and change?
Most whole-period hotspots were in central Myanmar. Recent increases extended across Kawkareik’s neighbours, while Kyaukpyu and Nawnghkio rose beside an average decline.


Which forms of violence increased?
Civilian-targeting air/drone and abduction events rose sharply. Declines in shelling and other categories left the civilian total only 2% lower.


Where did civilian targeting keep recurring?
Monywa, Kale and Pakokku recorded incidents through most of the 57 months. Monywa and Maungdaw still had incidents in eight of nine months in both recent years, despite lower counts.



The national decline was uneven in both place and form. Fewer total events could coexist with rising civilian targeting, as in Myaing and Pakokku. A falling count could also leave incidents recurring through most months, as in Monywa.
The monthly civilian analysis adds another distinction. Nawnghkio is a hotspot in both histories, while Kawkareik’s overall and civilian histories end differently. The reference check also changes some labels, including Kawkareik’s, even where the rising trend remains. Reading these labels alongside the counts gives a clearer account of what changed locally.
The published accounts help place these findings in context. ACLED describes changing tactics and armed-group relationships; the Rakhine fieldwork and OCHA reports describe daily restrictions and interrupted services. Together, they give a reason to consider the type and timing of violence when following up local needs. The event maps locate recorded changes, while local accounts are needed to understand their consequences for households.

title: Conflict across Myanmar’s townships
text:
Civilian targeting kept recurring

Monywa recorded civilian targeting in 53 of 57 months. Its January to September count fell from 61 to 31, yet events still covered 8 of nine months in both years. Maungdaw also had eight affected months in each year. In Myaing, reports spread from 5 months to 8.

Grey cells mean no civilian-targeting event was recorded. Monywa had 29 civilian hotspot months but ended with “No pattern detected”. Recurrence counts any recorded incident; EHSA tests whether neighbourhood counts are unusually high or low.

title: Hands-on Exercise 8
text:
1 Overview
The Huff model combines store attractiveness and travel distance. A larger or closer store receives a higher patronage probability from each village.

1.1 Learning Outcome
I prepare the store, population and sales data, build a village-to-store distance matrix, estimate patronage probabilities, and compare estimated demand with recorded sales.


1.2 Setting the scene
People can choose among several stores, so market areas rarely stop at administrative boundaries. The model gives every village-store pair a probability, allowing one village to contribute to several store markets.


1.3 The data
The data cover 28 stores, Taichung’s town and village boundaries, village populations from 2019, and store sales records.

title: Hands-on Exercise 8
text:
5 Computing Distance Matrix
I represent each village by a point inside its polygon, then calculate the straight-line distance from every village point to every store.

village_center <- st_point_on_surface(village)
distmat <- st_distance(village_center, stores) 


rownames(distmat) <- village$`VILLCODE`
colnames(distmat) <- stores$`Store_CD`

distmat_long <- distmat %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "VILLCODE") %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -VILLCODE,
    names_to = "Store_CD",
    values_to = "distance"
  ) %>%
  mutate(distance = as.numeric(distance))

title: Hands-on Exercise 8
text:
6 Preparing Interaction Matrix

interaction_matrix <- distmat_long %>%
  left_join(
    stores %>% 
      st_drop_geometry() %>% 
      select(Store_CD, Store_size),
    by = "Store_CD") %>%
  relocate(
    distance, .after = last_col())

title: Hands-on Exercise 8
text:
7 Computing Huff model

huff_share <- huff.shares(
  interaction_matrix, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD", 
  "Store_size", "distance")


7.1 Trade area analysis for a single store
I use Store BT to see how its patronage probability changes across villages.

market_share <- huff_share %>%
  filter(Store_CD == "BT")


Trade_area <- village %>%
  left_join(market_share)


selected_store <- stores %>%
  filter(Store_CD == "BT")


tm_shape(Trade_area) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_ij",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Patronage Probability")) +
  tm_shape(selected_store) +
    tm_dots(size = 0.3,
            fill = "red",
            col = "black") +
  tm_title("Distribution of Patronage Probability of Store BT by village") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha =0.2) 










7.2 Store sales analysis
I add each village’s population to the patronage probabilities to estimate the customers each store can attract.

huff_share_pp <- huff_share %>%
  left_join(village %>% 
      st_drop_geometry() %>% 
      select(VILLCODE, P_CNT),
    by = "VILLCODE") %>%
  relocate(
    distance, .after = last_col())


huff_total <- shares.total(
  huff_share_pp, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
  "p_ij", "P_CNT")


store_sales_est <- stores %>%
  left_join(huff_total,
            by = join_by(
              "Store_CD" == "suppliers_single"))


store_sales_nongeom <- store_sales_est %>% 
  st_drop_geometry()

ggscatterstats(
  store_sales_nongeom,
  x = sum_E_j,
  y = Total_Sales)









huff_share_wider <- huff_share %>%
  select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, p_ij) %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = Store_CD, 
                values_from = p_ij)

title: Hands-on Exercise 8
text:
8 Takeaways
The Huff model gives each store a gradual market area. Store BT has higher patronage probabilities in nearby villages, and its probability falls where rival stores are more attractive or easier to reach.
The final comparison shows how closely the population-based estimate follows recorded sales. Store format, prices, transport routes and local shopping habits may explain the remaining difference.

title: Conflict across Myanmar’s townships
text:
Civilian hotspots have different histories




The civilian map shows 25 hotspot townships with a significant trend. Mandalay and Magway contain 16 of them.
Nawnghkio is a sporadic hotspot in both the overall and civilian analyses.
Kawkareik’s civilian history ends with “No pattern detected”, despite its overall hotspot label. Its civilian trend also depends on the comparison period.
Kyaukpyu’s upward civilian trend survives both references and the stricter trend tests. Nawnghkio’s rise becomes less certain when those checks are applied together.

The two-month reference retains 86.9% of civilian EHSA classes. With the whole-period reference, allowing for related months reduces significant trends from 186 to 123; 93 survive multiple-test adjustment. Full comparison
